                                       PROJECT NO. 58481


 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT LARGE                          §          PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LOAD INTERCONNECTION STANDARDS                         §
                                                                                 OF TEXAS
 UNDER PURA 37.0561                                     §



                  COMMENTS OF CROSS TEXAS TRANSMISSION, LLC

Cross Texas Transmission, LLC (“CTT”) submits these comments in response to the
Commission’s proposal to establish a structured process for the interconnection of large loads
within ERCOT. CTT appreciates the Public Utility Commission of Texas’s (“Commission”)
leadership in addressing issues that have grown in urgency as Texas experiences extraordinary
large load growth. Staff’s Discussion Draft represents a substantial and thoughtful effort to provide
ERCOT, interconnecting electric utilities, and market participants with clearer expectations and a
more predictable framework for evaluating and studying very large new loads.

CTT offers these comments not as objections to the Commission’s objectives, but to ensure that
the final rule is both durable and practicable for interconnecting electric utilities that must
implement it. Texas is experiencing an unprecedented shift in load characteristics, with new
demand fundamentally different in magnitude and operational profile from historic norms.
Integrating these loads requires a process that appropriately screens speculative inquiries, while
still enabling legitimate, well-capitalized projects to advance. As drafted, the rule affects not only
initial customer commitments but also several core responsibilities borne by interconnecting
electric utilities, including study obligations, project scheduling, procurement of long-lead
equipment, coordination with ERCOT, and long-term operational reliability.

The rule also intersects with foundational issues of transmission investment and cost recovery.
Electric utilities are being asked to study, construct, and own facilities that will remain part of the
ERCOT transmission system for decades. It is essential that any final rule preserve electric
utilities’ ability to timely invest in, recover the costs of, and earn a reasonable return on
transmission facilities required to accommodate large load interconnections supporting Texas’s
evolving economy.
                                                                                                 2 of 8


•       Introduction and Background

CTT supports the Commission’s objective of improving predictability and establishing clearer
expectations for the interconnection of large loads. Texas faces unprecedented interest from data
centers, AI-driven computing clusters, hydrogen production facilities, industrial electrification,
and petrochemical expansion. ERCOT’s public data reflect more than 230 GW of potential large
load requests, volumes far exceeding anything previously seen in the region. A more structured
process is warranted.

However, certain provisions of the proposed rule, absent further revision, risk inadvertently
undermining the Commission's stated objectives. These issues fall into two broad categories: (1)
foundational financial and policy matters and (2) practical implementation issues that directly
affect electric utilities tasked with administering the rule.

First, the magnitude and timing of financial commitments, including the requirement to provide
security at $50,000 per MW and non-refundable contributions in aid of construction (“CIAC”) for
all interconnection-related facilities, may exclude otherwise viable projects. A rule designed to
screen speculative requests should not inadvertently screen out viable projects.

Second, the draft rule does not distinguish between customer-specific interconnection facilities
and transmission system upgrades that become permanent components of the ERCOT grid.
Treating these fundamentally different facilities the same for cost-recovery purposes creates a
misalignment between ownership responsibilities and financing, and it obscures the role of
ERCOT’s planning processes in identifying upgrades that serve broader system needs. The rule
should preserve ERCOT’s ability to determine, through established regional planning processes,
which upgrades are systemwide and which are customer specific. Not all upgrades triggered in a
study arise solely from, or provide benefits solely to, the requesting load. Over-attributing upgrade
costs to first movers could distort siting decisions and undermine efficient development.

Third, the rule as written requires interconnecting electric utilities to own and maintain facilities
that customers must fully fund through CIAC. This disconnects ownership from financing and
cost recovery. Under longstanding principles articulated in Hope and Bluefield, utilities must have
the opportunity to recover their investments and earn a return sufficient to attract capital. The
                                                                                                3 of 8


proposed structure risks misalignment that could impair long-term transmission development
unless the Commission includes a funding option for interconnecting electric utilities.

These considerations present the Commission with an opportunity to adopt a durable, balanced
framework that supports reliable interconnection, appropriately filters speculative requests, and
preserves the investment signals and operational structures needed to serve unprecedented new
load in ERCOT.

•      Texas Has a Proven Record of Integrating Large Loads and Should Reinforce That
       Strength

Texas has historically been one of the most successful jurisdictions in the country at integrating
new load, in large part because ERCOT and its electric utilities have maintained a planning and
interconnection framework that balances rigor with flexibility. CTT’s experience in the Panhandle
and Brazos Valley demonstrates that ERCOT’s planning processes and study methodologies
already facilitate timely identification of system impacts and necessary upgrades.              The
collaborative interaction among ERCOT planners, electric utility engineers, and customer
representatives promotes practical solutions tailored to the unique characteristics of each request.

Projects such as the recently approved portions of ERCOT’s 765 kV Strategic Transmission
Expansion Plan (STEP) illustrate Texas’s ability to anticipate forward-looking needs. These
achievements depend on reliable cost recovery, stable regulatory structures, and the ability of
electric utilities to finance facilities subject to Commission oversight.

The proposed rule should build on this foundation. The Commission does not need to re-engineer
ERCOT’s planning processes to address the challenges at hand. Instead, it should reinforce the
proven elements of the Texas model while refining the elements that introduce misalignment or
unintended consequences.

•      The Proposed Collateral and CIAC Requirements Risk Excluding Legitimate
       Projects

CTT supports the Commission’s goal of discouraging speculative requests that consume study
resources and create uncertainty in ERCOT’s planning models. However, the combination of early
                                                                                                 4 of 8


deadlines, substantial financial obligations, and non-refundable CIAC requirements threatens to
suppress legitimate development rather than filter out non-serious inquiries.

A principal concern arises from ERCOT’s draft compliance plan, which contemplates requiring
customers to satisfy the rule’s financial commitment requirements by Apr. 1, 2026, in order to be
included in the next Resource Transmission Plan. Under the draft rule, customers must post
security at $50,000 per MW to demonstrate financial commitment early in the interconnection
process and, thereafter, provide non-refundable CIAC covering all expected costs of
interconnection facilities and system upgrades.        Together, these layered requirements can
necessitate substantial non-refundable capital commitments on a highly compressed timeline for
projects that are often multi-billion dollars in scale. If applied as drafted, these requirements may
exclude precisely the types of projects that Texas is seeking to attract. This would not simply delay
individual projects. It would distort ERCOT’s planning models and reduce the predictability that
the rule aims to achieve.

It is important to note that CTT is not proposing to eliminate the $50,000 per MW security
requirement. Our concern is about how and when these financial commitments are imposed. As
drafted, the rule requires large security payments at the very outset of development and ties them
to an ERCOT planning deadline that forces premature capital deployment. CTT recommends that
collateral obligations be aligned with realistic project milestones. Readiness screening should rely
on substantive indicators of project maturity including site control, permitting progress,
engineering development, and commercial commitments rather than a customer’s near-term
liquidity or ability to post millions of dollars within a compressed window of time.

•      The Commission Should Distinguish Between Customer-Specific Interconnection
       Facilities and System Upgrades

CTT believes the Commission should distinguish between the two categories of facilities
implicated by the draft rule. Under 16 Texas Administrative Code § 25.194 as drafted, CIAC
applies to both customer-specific interconnection facilities and system upgrades “that would not
be required but for” the interconnecting large load.
                                                                                                5 of 8


Customer interconnection facilities, such as dedicated radial lines or customer-specific substation
bays, are appropriately treated as sole-use assets for which the large load customer should bear
100 percent of the cost through CIAC. By contrast, system upgrades triggered by a large load
including new substations, networked transmission lines, or reinforcements that become part of
the ERCOT networked grid are also required to be fully CIAC-funded under the draft rule, even
though these facilities are long-lived assets that the interconnecting electric utility must operate
and maintain as part of the regional transmission system.

Treating system facilities in the same manner as customer-specific interconnection facilities
creates a misalignment between ownership, operational responsibility, and cost recovery.

•      The Commission Should Allow Interconnecting Electric Utilities to Fund System
       Upgrades

As an initial matter, CTT emphasizes that any funding election by interconnecting electric utilities
would apply only to system upgrades that become part of the ERCOT transmission system. Sole
use customer-specific interconnection facilities would continue to be fully CIAC-funded,
consistent with the draft rule.

As drafted, the rule requires interconnecting electric utilities to operate and maintain all
interconnection facilities and system upgrades, yet it contemplates that these facilities will be
financed entirely through customer-funded CIAC. This structure disconnects the risks associated
with long-term ownership and operational responsibility for system upgrades from the financing
of those assets.

An interconnecting electric utility that must operate and maintain a facility for decades must also
have access to predictable cost recovery at just and reasonable terms. Customer-funded CIAC for
system upgrades removes the investment from ratebase and prevents the interconnecting electric
utility from earning a regulated return, even though it bears the ongoing responsibility and risks
for maintaining reliability and ensuring safe operation. Even with receiving customer-funded
CIAC, interconnecting electric utilities would still need to maintain compliance with reliability
standards, carry potential liability for insurance deductibles and litigation stemming from personal
injury, manage environmental risk, and more.
                                                                                                6 of 8


Allowing the interconnecting electric utilities to fund the system upgrades would address this
misalignment by permitting the interconnecting electric utility to finance and ratebase system
upgrades that it is required to operate and maintain. This approach aligns ownership, operational
responsibility, and financing of long-lived system assets in a manner consistent with traditional
utility regulation.

This funding mechanism is not without precedent. Under both the Midcontinent ISO’s and the
Southwest Power Pool’s Open Access Transmission Tariff, transmission owners have the right to
elect a Transmission Owner Initial Funding Option for network (system) upgrades associated with
new generation interconnections. This model was upheld by the D.C. Circuit in Ameren Services
Co. v. FERC, where the court held that depriving utilities of the ability to earn a return on assets
that they are required to own violated the principles articulated by the U.S. Supreme Court in Hope
and Bluefield. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission reinstated the Transmission Owner
Initial Funding option on remand, recognizing that utilities cannot be expected to assume long-
lived obligations without corresponding financial mechanisms.

•       System Upgrades Should Continue to Be Determined Through ERCOT’s Regional
        Planning Function

CTT supports the Commission’s desire for clarity around the allocation of interconnection costs.
However, the rule should not embed presumptions about causation for system upgrades that arise
in the course of a large-load study. Not all upgrades identified in such studies are driven solely by
the requested load. Many reflect aggregate growth, geographic clustering, evolving renewable
buildout, or long-term economic patterns. Even where a large load is a “but for” cause of a
transmission system upgrade, such transmission system upgrades often enhance reliability, transfer
capability, and operational flexibility across the transmission system, producing benefits that
extend well beyond the point of interconnection. Requiring the interconnection customer alone to
bear the full cost of such upgrades misaligns cost responsibility with systemwide benefits and
undermines the principle that transmission costs should be allocated broadly to the customers who
benefit from them.

ERCOT’s regional planning processes are best equipped to determine which upgrades serve a
broader set of customers and should therefore be treated as system projects rather than customer-
                                                                                                7 of 8


specific reinforcements.     Preserving this framework avoids penalizing first movers and
discouraging efficient siting.

•      Multiple Layers of Financial Security Create Operational and Sequencing Challenges
       for Interconnecting Electric Utilities

The draft rule requires, sequentially: (1) a study fee; (2) financial security at $50,000 per MW; (3)
additional security equal to the cost of long-lead equipment; and (4) full CIAC before construction.

While each element has a purpose, together they create a series of gating events around which the
interconnecting electric utility must plan procurement, engineering, and construction activities.
Any failure by the customer to meet a payment deadline obligates the interconnecting electric
utility to halt work, unwind processes, and adjust internal planning. These interruptions increase
cost and introduce uncertainty into interconnecting electric utility operations.

CTT recognizes the Commission’s interest in ensuring that only credible projects progress through
the interconnection process. CTT believes the rule would benefit from greater alignment between
financial obligations and substantive indicators of project maturity. Readiness measures such as
site control, permitting progress, and engineering development offer a more informed and durable
basis for screening than liquidity alone, and we encourage the Commission to consider how these
factors could inform the timing and structure of financial commitments.

•      Conclusion

CTT appreciates the Commission’s commitment to establishing a structured, transparent, and
reliable process for integrating very large loads into the ERCOT system. Texas is entering a period
of transformative load growth, and the rule adopted in this proceeding will strongly influence
where and how that growth can be served. It will also shape transmission investment patterns and
operational obligations for decades.

The comments above identify several refinements that CTT believes are necessary to ensure the
rule fulfills its intended purpose. These include aligning collateral and CIAC requirements with
commercial development realities; distinguishing between customer-specific interconnection
facilities and transmission system upgrades for purposes of cost recovery; incorporating a funding
                                                                                                   8 of 8


option for interconnecting electric utilities to preserve the fundamental relationship between utility
ownership and cost recovery; and maintaining ERCOT’s central role in distinguishing customer-
specific reinforcements from broader system needs.

With these refinements, the Commission can adopt a policy framework that supports ERCOT
reliability, fosters efficient interconnection of legitimate projects, and enables electric utilities to
meet their long-term obligations in a financially sustainable manner.           CTT appreciates the
opportunity to provide these comments and looks forward to continued engagement with the
Commission Staff and ERCOT as this rulemaking proceeds.

                                                               Respectfully submitted,

                                                                 /s/ Terry Harvill

                                                               Terry Harvill
                                                               Vice President, Transmission
                                                               Regulatory

                                                               West Lake Hills, TX 78746

Executive Summary


Cross Texas Transmission, LLC (“CTT”) respectfully recommends that the Commission consider
the following in adopting any final rule in this proceeding:


•   Align the timing and structure of financial commitment requirements with realistic
    project development milestones.
    The magnitude and sequencing of required financial commitments, including security at
    $50,000 per MW and subsequent non-refundable contributions in aid of construction
    (“CIAC”), may impose substantial capital commitments on a highly compressed timeline.
    Financial commitment requirements should be structured to support ERCOT’s objective of
    screening speculative projects without inadvertently excluding viable projects.


•   Distinguish between customer-specific interconnection facilities and transmission
    system upgrades.
    Customer-specific interconnection facilities are appropriately funded through CIAC. By
    contrast, transmission system upgrades that become permanent components of the ERCOT
    transmission system should be identified and addressed through ERCOT’s established
    regional planning processes, which are best suited to determine whether such upgrades serve
    broader system needs.


•   Preserve the ability of electric utilities to invest in and earn a reasonable return on
    transmission system upgrades.
    Where electric utilities are required to construct, own, and operate long-lived transmission
    system upgrades to accommodate large load interconnections, the regulatory framework must
    preserve the opportunity for utilities to recover their investment and earn a return
    commensurate with the risks assumed. Allowing a funding option for system upgrades
    would better align ownership, operational responsibility, and financing with traditional utility
    regulation.
 Cross Texas Transmission, LLC


CTT appreciates the opportunity to provide these comments and looks forward to continued
engagement with the Commission and ERCOT as this rulemaking proceeds.
